section_1.title: Intuitive Prerequisite: The Antipodal Mapping
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of a sphere (S²) and the 'antipodal point'—the point exactly on the opposite side of a sphere. Visualize this as placing a glowing point on the North Pole and its twin on the South Pole.
section_1.example: Imagine a world map wrapped on a sphere. If you stand at the North Pole, your antipode is the South Pole.

section_2.title: The Core Concept: Borsuk-Ulam Theorem
section_2.content: Explain the theorem: Any continuous mapping from an n-sphere to n-dimensional Euclidean space must map at least one pair of antipodal points to the same location. Focus on the 2D case (S² to R²).
section_2.example: Visual animation: A globe with varying temperature/pressure data. The theorem guarantees there are at least two opposite points on Earth right now with the exact same temperature and air pressure.

section_3.title: The Stolen Necklace Problem
section_3.content: Transition to the application: Two thieves steal a necklace with different types of beads. They must divide the loot so that each gets an equal share of every type of bead. The necklace can be cut at most k times (where k is the number of bead types).
section_3.example: A visual chain of 10 gold beads and 10 silver beads. An animation shows the necklace being 'unfolded' into a line, and the cuts being made to distribute beads equally between two characters, 'Alice' and 'Bob'.

section_4.title: Bridging Theory and Problem
section_4.content: Explain how the necklace is modeled as an interval, then mapped to a sphere, allowing the Borsuk-Ulam theorem to prove that a fair division exists mathematically, even if finding the cuts is computationally difficult.
section_4.example: Use a 'color-coded bar' animation where segments shift until the Borsuk-Ulam condition is satisfied, showing the 'Fair Division' point being reached.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Summary
section_5.content: Summarize that Borsuk-Ulam is a powerful existence theorem in topology. It doesn't tell us where to cut, but it guarantees that a perfectly fair 'theft' is always possible.
section_5.example: Final slide: 'Topology: Proving the impossible exists, even when we can't find it easily.'

        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

        mobject.move_to(center)

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Thieves divide a necklace with different beads.",
            "They want an equal share of every bead type.",
            "We can cut the necklace at most k times."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Stolen Necklace Problem", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display a necklace represented by a line of colored beads
        beads = VGroup(*[Circle(radius=0.2, color=color, fill_opacity=1) for color in [GOLD, BLUE]*5])
        beads.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        self.place_at_grid(beads, 'C2')
        self.play(FadeIn(beads))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Show two thieves dividing segments to equalize the value
        alice = Text("Alice", color=BLUE, font_size=20)
        bob = Text("Bob", color=GOLD, font_size=20)
        self.place_at_grid(alice, 'A3')
        self.place_at_grid(bob, 'E3')
        
        # Split beads
        split_beads = VGroup(beads[:5].copy(), beads[5:].copy())
        self.play(
            FadeOut(beads),
            FadeIn(alice),
            FadeIn(bob),
            split_beads[0].animate.move_to(self.grid['B3']),
            split_beads[1].animate.move_to(self.grid['D3'])
        )
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#33FF57")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Animate cutting the necklace
        cut = Line(UP*0.5, DOWN*0.5, color=RED)
        cut.move_to(self.grid['C3'])
        self.play(Create(cut))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF5733")
        self.wait(1)
